clinicalPearls: Autosomal dominant motor neuronopathy in which weakness and wasting predominate in the lower limbs, particularly the proximal thigh and quadriceps muscles
Caused by variants in DYNC1H1 (the heavy chain of cytoplasmic dynein) or BICD2 (a dynein-adaptor protein), both essential for retrograde axonal transport
Often presents in early childhood with delayed walking, a waddling gait and difficulty rising, and may appear relatively static over long periods
Predominant proximal lower-limb involvement with relative sparing of the upper limbs helps distinguish it from length-dependent neuropathies
Some DYNC1H1 cases have associated cortical malformations and learning difficulty, reflecting the wider role of dynein in the developing brain
Electrophysiology shows a motor neuronopathy pattern with chronic denervation and preserved sensory responses
Diagnosis requires the lower-limb-predominant distribution together with genetic confirmation of a DYNC1H1 or BICD2 variant
reference.pathophysiology: Lower-extremity-predominant spinal muscular atrophy is a dominant motor neurone disorder caused by variants in components of the cytoplasmic dynein transport machinery: DYNC1H1 encodes the dynein heavy chain and BICD2 encodes an adaptor that links dynein to its cargo. Disruption of dynein-mediated retrograde axonal transport impairs the delivery of signalling molecules and organelles within motor neurones, leading to degeneration that preferentially affects the neurones supplying proximal lower-limb muscles. The result is a largely static or slowly progressive lower motor neurone weakness with preserved sensation. Because dynein is also crucial to neuronal migration, some DYNC1H1 variants additionally cause brain malformation and cognitive impairment.
additionalDifferentials: Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy with proximal weakness
Hereditary spastic paraplegia when there is a lower-limb-predominant picture
Other distal or proximal hereditary motor neuropathies
additionalInvestigations: Electromyography and nerve conduction studies showing chronic motor neuronopathy with preserved sensation
DYNC1H1 and BICD2 sequencing or a hereditary neuromuscular panel
SMN1 testing to exclude 5q spinal muscular atrophy
Creatine kinase and muscle imaging to help separate neurogenic from myopathic weakness
Brain MRI where cortical malformation or learning difficulty is present
Detailed family history for dominant inheritance
redFlags: Prominent upper motor neurone signs suggesting an alternative diagnosis
Seizures or significant developmental regression pointing to associated brain malformation
Rapidly progressive weakness inconsistent with a largely static disorder
Respiratory involvement, which is atypical and warrants review
reference.prognosis: Often relatively static or only slowly progressive, with many patients remaining ambulant into adulthood; prognosis is more guarded in DYNC1H1 cases complicated by brain malformation and cognitive impairment.
pitfalls: Mistaking proximal lower-limb weakness for a primary muscle disease without electrophysiology
Not testing DYNC1H1/BICD2 after a negative SMN1 result
Overlooking associated cortical malformation and learning difficulty in DYNC1H1 disease
Assuming steady progression when the course is frequently static
references: GeneReviews: DYNC1H1- and BICD2-Related Spinal Muscular Atrophy
Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
management: Provide supportive care centred on physiotherapy to maintain lower-limb strength, range of motion and gait, as there is no gene-specific disease-modifying therapy
Prescribe orthoses such as ankle-foot orthoses and mobility aids to support proximal lower-limb weakness and reduce falls
Manage foot deformity and contractures with orthopaedic input and, where indicated, corrective surgery
Screen DYNC1H1 patients for associated cortical malformation and learning difficulty with brain MRI and neurodevelopmental support where indicated
Monitor the largely static to slowly progressive course with periodic functional and respiratory assessment
Distinguish from 5q spinal muscular atrophy by SMN1 testing so that prognosis and management are correctly framed
Offer genetic counselling for autosomal dominant inheritance and cascade testing of relatives
